newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico still a draw to foreign retailers -analysts.
newsitem.headline: Mexico still a draw to foreign retailers -analysts.

text.p: Recent moves by U.S. retailers Kmart Corp and Sears, Roebuck and Co to sell their Mexico businesses do not mean foreign retailers are losing their appetite for the country, analysts say.

Dozens of other firms, including U.S. retailing giant Wal-Mart and French firms Auchan and Carrefour, are pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Mexico to tap into a growing market of 90 million consumers.

"It would be mistaken to interpret the moves by Kmart and Sears as a pull-out of Mexico. There are still a lot of foreign retailers investing heavily," Alberto Montagne, an analyst at Lehman Brothers in New York, told Reuters.
"What is happening is a consolidation process. Weeding out the bad from the good as the Mexican market grows," he added.
Kmart last week sold its joint venture company Kmart de Mexico to Controladora Comercial Mexicana, the country's second-largest retailer.
Days later, Sears Roebuck sold almost all of its Mexican holdings to conglomerate Grupo Carso. Sears had been in Mexico since the mid-1940s.

Both retailers pared their Mexican operations, which were still smarting from the country's 1995 recession, to focus on their core U.S. businesses. But both also had troubles in Mexico that were specific to each company, analysts said.
Kmart's venture in Mexico was flawed from the start because it teamed up with El Puerto de Liverpool, a department store operator that has little in common with the U.S. retailer, analysts said.

"There were very few synergies between the two. Kmart was unable to take advantage of economies of scale and bulk purchasing discounts from Liverpool's suppliers," said Rolando Calderon, an analyst at Santander Investment in Mexico City.

Sears de Mexico, which lost money for eight consecutive quarters, suffered from bad management and poor positioning in the market, analysts said. Its parent company found it was unable to control the Mexican firm closely.
"Sears' trouble had more to do with management than a bad economy. Its sales were not bad, but its administrative expenses were much higher compared to other Mexican retailers," Calderon said.

The fact that Sears' Mexico unit was bought by Carso owner Carlos Slim, a billionaire known here for his business acumen, could mean Slim is betting on a recovery in the retail sector later this year that will prove he bought at the right time.
Other foreign-owned companies seem to agree with Slim's strategy to buy ahead of an expected recovery.

Carrefour's ambitious expansion plans in Mexico forced it to suspend in part a joint venture with Gigante because the Mexican firm could not raise enough money to match the French retailer's investment.
Wal-Mart, which plans to open eight Wal-Mart Supercenters in Mexico this year, also is expected to expand its joint venture with the country's largest retailer Cifra SA.

Privately-held Auchan will probably spend more than $100 million this year in opening new hyper-market stores while Texas-based supermarket chain HEB plans to open two giant supermarkets in the northern city of Monterrey, analysts said.
"The recovery in (Mexico's) retail sector has been slower than expected, but it is starting to heat up. And those making the deals now will be the big winners later," Calderon said.
The recent flurry of activity is likely to continue as local firms look to foreign partners for expertise and outsiders aim for a Mexican partner will local know-how.
And analysts said there could be interesting activity among local firms as smaller stores consolidate to compete with larger rivals.
